query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. One such class comprises the RHEAs which, because of their high melting points, have been proposed as candidates for ultrahigh-temperature applications. However, a single-phase RHEA, TiZrHfNbTa, was recently shown to be significantly weaker in creep than CMSX-4 despite the former’s higher melting point. The weakness was ascribed to two factors: faster diffusion in the BCC matrix of the RHEA relative to the FCC matrix of CMSX-4 and a lack of precipitates. Additional research is therefore needed to enhance the creep strength of TiZrHfNbTa, for example, by the introduction of suitable strengthening precipitates. Meanwhile, RHEAs with higher melting points must also be investigated since diffusion will be slower in such materials. One such RHEA is VNbMoTaW, whose melting point is ~500 °C higher than TiZrHfNbTa,,. However, it has a major disadvantage: lack of ductility at room temperature even in compression. In contrast, TiZrHfNbTa exhibits ductility at room temperature both in compression and in tension (~8%), albeit not as much as the highly ductile and fracture-resistant FCC HEAs. Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

decision.trend: Research has focused on improving the room-temperature ductility of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) without compromising their high-temperature mechanical performance. Various strategies have been explored, including microstructural engineering, thermomechanical treatments, and alloy design. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of the ratio of HCP to BCC elements in controlling ductility and strength in RHEAs.
decision.unsolved: The poor room-temperature ductility of RHEAs remains a significant challenge, and further research is needed to develop effective strategies for improving their ductility without compromising their high-temperature performance.
decision.why: The addition of HCP elements to BCC RHEAs has been shown to enhance ductility by lowering dislocation core energy, increasing lattice distortion, and reducing shear modulus. This approach offers a promising route for optimizing the mechanical properties of RHEAs for ultrahigh-temperature applications.
